Isaiah 14
eye-ZAY-uh FOR-teen
proper noun
The fourteenth chapter of Isaiah; the taunt-song over the fallen king of Babylon, with its “Lucifer, son of the morning.”

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 14 is the prophet’s taunt-song over the fall of the king of Babylon, the proud oppressor brought down to the grave, and one of the most searching passages in Scripture on the ruin that pride works. The LORD promises rest to His people from their bondage, and then puts in their mouth a proverb against the tyrant: How hath the oppressor ceased! The whole earth is at rest, and the very trees of the forest rejoice that no feller is come up against them. Hell from beneath is moved to meet him; the kings of the nations rise from their thrones to greet the once-mighty king now made weak as they. Then comes the famous cry: How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! For he had said in his heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, I will be like the most High—the five great “I wills” of pride—yet he is brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit. The dictionary reads the chapter first of the historical king of Babylon, the proud tyrant judged by God; and, as the church has long discerned in the language of a creature reaching to be like the most High, an apt picture of the pride of Satan and the sure ruin of all who exalt themselves against God.

Webster 1828 Definition

The fourteenth chapter of Isaiah; the taunt over the fallen king of Babylon—the five “I wills” of pride and the ruin of the oppressor brought down to the pit.

Key Scripture

Isa 14:12 — "How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning! how art thou cut down to the ground, which didst weaken the nations!"

Isa 14:13 — "For thou hast said in thine heart, I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God: I will sit also upon the mount of the congregation, in the sides of the north:"

Isa 14:14 — "I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will be like the most High."

Isa 14:15 — "Yet thou shalt be brought down to hell, to the sides of the pit."

Modern Corruption

Modern critics flatten the chapter to mere ancient political rhetoric and deny any reference beyond the human king; the church reads it of the Babylonian tyrant and discerns in it the pride and ruin of Satan.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the chapter’s reference. Its first and plain sense is the historical king of Babylon, the proud oppressor of God’s people, judged and brought down to the grave; modern critical readers who allow only this human reference are right as far as they go but wrong to forbid more. The church has long discerned, in the language of a being who would ascend above the stars of God and be like the most High and is cast down to the pit, an apt picture of the pride of Satan—the creature’s reach to usurp the Creator’s throne. The dictionary holds both: the Babylonian tyrant in the foreground, and behind him the ancient pride that fell from heaven.

The principle to recover is the certain ruin of pride that exalts itself against God. The five “I wills” of the chapter are the very grammar of rebellion—I will ascend, I will exalt, I will be like the most High—and they end in the sides of the pit. Whether in Babylon’s king, in the fallen accuser, or in the proud heart of any man, the lesson is one: God resists the proud, and everyone that exalteth himself shall be abased.
